In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of physics-based modeling of electron mobility in ultrashort-channel MOSFETs.
the development of physics-based modeling for the simulation of III-V MOSFETs.
the development of a physics-based model of the electron mobility in InGaAs-oninsulator MOSFET devices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

InGaAs MOSFETs have the potential to outperform Si MOSFETs in the sub-10-nm gate length regime, provided that the quality of the InGaAs/oxide interface is comparable or better to that of the Si/SiO _{2} interface.
InGaAs on insulator is an interesting option for high-speed and low-power applications, but the interface quality has to be improved to achieve the full potential of this material.
InGaAs MOSFETs with a body thickness of 5–10 nm and an interface state density of 1×1012/cm2 are a viable alternative to silicon MOSFETs, provided the channel is not too short.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

InGaAs MOSFETs can be a good candidate for future high-performance CMOS devices only in case of a significant improvement in the interface quality, which is a challenge in the current III-V technology.
InGaAs-based devices can be competitive with Si-based ones only if they are fabricated using a high-quality interface and the thickness of the channel is above the critical value.

The main takeaway from our work is that
, in addition to the interface quality, thickness fluctuations are an important parameter that needs to be considered when designing InGaAs-based FETs.
